# errno

Reading C's thread-local `errno`, and which C runtime it lives in.

<h2 id="c-runtime"><code>CRuntime</code></h2>

```rux
// Windows
pub const CRuntime = "ucrtbase.dll";

// Linux
pub const CRuntime = "libc.so.6";

// macOS
pub const CRuntime = "libSystem.B.dylib";

// FreeBSD
pub const CRuntime = "libc.so.7";
```

The shared object this target's C runtime lives in.

[Source](https://github.com/rux-lang/Rux/blob/main/Packages/C/Src/Types.rux#L210)

<h2 id="stream-runtime"><code>StreamRuntime</code></h2>

```rux
// Windows
pub const StreamRuntime = "msvcrt.dll";

// Linux
pub const StreamRuntime = "libc.so.6";

// macOS
pub const StreamRuntime = "libSystem.B.dylib";

// FreeBSD
pub const StreamRuntime = "libc.so.7";
```

The shared object `C::StdIo` and `C::Time` are bound to, which on Windows is a different one.
The Universal CRT does not export the formatted-output family, so those two modules bind the legacy
runtime. It keeps its own `errno`, its own stream table and its own locale, so a failure reported by a
call through either module is readable only through `ErrnoFor(CRuntimeArea::Streams)`.

| Overload                                         | Summary                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pub const StreamRuntime = "msvcrt.dll";`        | The shared object `C::StdIo` and `C::Time` are bound to, which on Windows is a different one.  |
| `pub const StreamRuntime = "libc.so.6";`         | The shared object `C::StdIo` and `C::Time` are bound to, which on this target is the same one. |
| `pub const StreamRuntime = "libSystem.B.dylib";` | The shared object `C::StdIo` and `C::Time` are bound to, which on this target is the same one. |
| `pub const StreamRuntime = "libc.so.7";`         | The shared object `C::StdIo` and `C::Time` are bound to, which on this target is the same one. |

[Source](https://github.com/rux-lang/Rux/blob/main/Packages/C/Src/Types.rux#L217)

<h2 id="c-runtime-area"><code>CRuntimeArea</code></h2>

```rux
pub enum CRuntimeArea: uint8 {
    General = 0,
    Streams = 1
}
```

Which of the package's C runtimes a call belongs to.
On Windows this package spans two: `StdLib` and `Math` bind the Universal CRT, while `StdIo` and `Time` bind the
legacy runtime, because the Universal CRT does not export the formatted-output family. The two keep separate
`errno` storage, so reading one after a call into the other reports a value belonging to something else
entirely.
Everywhere else there is one runtime and both cases name it, so a caller that always passes the area matching
the module it called is right on all four systems and needs no target branch of its own.

[Source](https://github.com/rux-lang/Rux/blob/main/Packages/C/Src/Types.rux#L283)

**Cases**

| Name      | Value | Description                                                                                         |
| --------- | ----- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `General` | `0`   | Where `C::StdLib` and `C::Math` are bound, and what plain [`Errno`](/docs/api/c/errno#errno) reads. |
| `Streams` | `1`   | Where `C::StdIo` and `C::Time` are bound. The same runtime as `General` except on Windows.          |

<h2 id="separate-stream-runtime"><code>SeparateStreamRuntime</code></h2>

```rux
pub const SeparateStreamRuntime: bool = #target.os == OperatingSystem::Windows;
```

Whether the two areas are really two runtimes on this target.
True on Windows and false everywhere else. A caller that passes the right area never needs to read this; it is
here so that a program can say why it is being careful, and so that a test can assert the split exists where it
is supposed to and does not where it is not.

[Source](https://github.com/rux-lang/Rux/blob/main/Packages/C/Src/Types.rux#L295)

<h2 id="errno-location-for"><code>ErrnoLocationFor</code></h2>

```rux
pub func ErrnoLocationFor(area: CRuntimeArea) -> *var c_int
```

The address of the calling thread's `errno`, in the runtime `area` names.
Returns a pointer that runtime owns, valid for as long as the calling thread runs. Writing through it is how
C's `errno = 0` is spelled, which a caller does before a call whose failure is only reported through `errno`.
Pass the area matching the module whose call is being checked: `Streams` after anything from `C::StdIo` or
`C::Time`, `General` after anything from `C::StdLib` or `C::Math`. Passing the wrong one is not a compile error
and not a crash; it reads a different thread-local integer, which is the whole hazard this exists to remove.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
The address belongs to the calling thread and must not be handed to another one.

[Source](https://github.com/rux-lang/Rux/blob/main/Packages/C/Src/Types.rux#L308)

**Parameters**

| Name   | Type           | Description                      |
| ------ | -------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `area` | `CRuntimeArea` | which runtime's storage to reach |

**Returns**: the address of that runtime's `errno` for this thread

<h2 id="errno-for"><code>ErrnoFor</code></h2>

```rux
pub func ErrnoFor(area: CRuntimeArea) -> c_int
```

The calling thread's current `errno` value, in the runtime `area` names.
Meaningful only after a call that documents setting it: no C function clears `errno` on success, so a value left
over from an earlier failure is still there. Clear it through [`ErrnoLocationFor`](/docs/api/c/errno#errno-location-for) before the call whose failure
is to be read.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

[Source](https://github.com/rux-lang/Rux/blob/main/Packages/C/Src/Types.rux#L325)

**Parameters**

| Name   | Type           | Description                     |
| ------ | -------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `area` | `CRuntimeArea` | which runtime's storage to read |

**Returns**: that runtime's `errno` for this thread

<h2 id="errno-location"><code>ErrnoLocation</code></h2>

```rux
pub func ErrnoLocation() -> *var c_int
```

The address of the calling thread's `errno`, in the runtime `C::StdLib` and `C::Math` are bound to.
Exactly `ErrnoLocationFor(CRuntimeArea::General)`, and the spelling to use when the call being checked came from
one of those two modules. After a call from `C::StdIo` or `C::Time` on Windows this reads the wrong runtime's
storage, which is what [`ErrnoLocationFor`](/docs/api/c/errno#errno-location-for) exists to let a caller avoid.
Writing through it is how C's `errno = 0` is spelled, which a caller does before a call whose failure is only
reported through `errno`.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
The address belongs to the calling thread and must not be handed to another one.

[Source](https://github.com/rux-lang/Rux/blob/main/Packages/C/Src/Types.rux#L339)

**Returns**: the address of the general runtime's `errno` for this thread

<h2 id="errno"><code>Errno</code></h2>

```rux
pub func Errno() -> c_int
```

The calling thread's current `errno` value.
Takes nothing and returns the value by copy. Meaningful only after a call that documents setting it: no C function
clears `errno` on success, so a value left over from an earlier failure is still there. Clear it with
`*ErrnoLocation() = 0` before the call whose failure is to be read.
On Windows this reads the Universal CRT's `errno`, which is the one `C::StdLib` and `C::Math` set. `C::StdIo` and
`C::Time` are still bound to the legacy `msvcrt.dll`, whose `errno` is a different variable in a different
runtime, so a failure reported by a call in either of those modules is not visible here. That split is a known
defect: the Universal CRT does not export the formatted-output family, so moving those modules across needs the
`__stdio_common_*` entry points declared first.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

[Source](https://github.com/rux-lang/Rux/blob/main/Packages/C/Src/Types.rux#L355)

**Returns**: the general runtime's `errno` for this thread
